listenings.text: I train lawyers and executives before big meetings, and the first thing I teach them is to read the room. Before you speak, look at the faces. Are people leaning forward, or are they checking their phones? Is the chair of the committee taking notes, or has she stopped writing? These cues tell you more than any question. When the room is skeptical, it is usually a mistake to sound too certain. A small caveat, said early, tends to make people trust you more. And if you are not sure about a number, say so. An audience is likely to forgive a tentative answer. It is much less likely to forgive a confident answer that turns out to be wrong.

In my first year as a partner, I wrote a legal opinion that said a new tariff rule was illegal. Full stop. No caveats. Six months later, the court disagreed, and our client was not happy. Today I write differently. I say that the rule is likely to be challenged, and that the court will probably accept some of our arguments. I explain my assumptions, and I add a short disclaimer about the parts of the law that are still open. Some young lawyers think this sounds weak. It does not. Clients tend to trust an opinion that shows its limits. What they cannot accept is an expert who overstates his case and then has to explain why he was wrong.

reading.rtitle: Why the Best Experts Sound Less Certain
paras: Many professionals believe that a strong expert never shows doubt. In meetings, they speak in absolute terms: this will work, that rule is illegal, the market will grow. Research on how audiences judge experts suggests a different picture. People tend to trust speakers who show the limits of what they know, as long as the main message is clear. A small caveat, said at the right moment, often makes the rest of the argument sound more credible, not less.

Linguists call this hedging. Instead of saying that a project will fail, an experienced speaker says that it is likely to face problems, or that it could be argued that the risks are too high. Hedging is not the same as being vague. A good hedge is precise: it tells the audience exactly how sure you are and why. Lawyers, scientists and central bankers hedge all the time, because overstating a claim can be expensive. A judge, a journalist or a regulator will remember the one sentence that turned out to be wrong.

Hedging also depends on the room. Before speaking, good communicators gauge the audience: they watch the cues, such as body language, silence and the questions people ask. A skeptical room usually needs more caveats and clearer assumptions. A room that already agrees needs fewer, or the speaker may sound tentative. The skill is not to hedge every sentence. It is to know which claims need a hedge, and which ones you can say with full confidence.
